Options: B) System software managing hardware and software resources
Explanation: OS: core software managing computer hardware, software resources, and provides common services. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS. Without OS, a computer cannot function.

QuestionText: Which is NOT an example of an operating system?
Explanation: MS Word is an application software, not an OS. OS: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Chrome OS. Applications run on top of the OS.
GUI (Graphical User Interface): visual interface using icons, windows, menus, mouse. Makes computing accessible. vs CLI (Command Line Interface): text commands only. Windows, macOS = GUI.

Options: A) At the top of screen
B) At the bottom of screen
Explanation: Windows taskbar: at bottom by default (can be moved). Contains: Start button, pinned apps, running apps, notification area (system tray) with clock.

Options: C) Using multiple users at same time
Explanation: Multitasking: OS allows multiple programs to run simultaneously. CPU rapidly switches between programs creating illusion of simultaneous execution. Modern OS use preemptive multitasking.

Options: B) Systems requiring immediate, deterministic responses (medical devices, aircraft, robots)
Explanation: RTOS: processes data with strict timing constraints — must respond within guaranteed time. Used in: pacemakers, aircraft control, industrial robots, anti-lock brakes, air traffic control.

Options: B) Multiple computers working together as a single system
Explanation: Distributed OS: manages multiple networked computers appearing as one system. Resources shared transparently. Used in cloud computing, scientific computing clusters (Google, Amazon).

Options: A) Is a type of RAM
B) Uses hard disk space to extend apparent RAM
Explanation: Virtual memory: uses portion of hard disk as extension of RAM. When RAM full, less-used data swapped to disk (paging/swapping). Allows running programs larger than physical RAM. Slower than RAM.

Options: B) Files deleted from hard drive (not permanently deleted yet)
Explanation: Recycle Bin: temporary storage for deleted files. Files not permanently deleted until Recycle Bin is emptied. Allows recovery of accidentally deleted files. Shift+Delete bypasses Recycle Bin.

Options: B) Configuring system settings (display, sound, network, users, etc.)
Explanation: Control Panel: central hub for Windows settings. Configure: display, sound, network, hardware, user accounts, security, time/language, accessibility. In Windows 10, many settings moved to Settings app.

Options: B) Creating, scheduling, and terminating programs/processes
Explanation: Process management: OS creates process when program runs, schedules CPU time (scheduling algorithms), handles multiple processes, terminates processes. Task Manager shows running processes.

Options: B) The type and associated application of a file (.docx=Word, .jpg=image)
Explanation: File extension: letters after the dot indicating file type. .docx (Word), .xlsx (Excel), .pdf, .mp3 (audio), .mp4 (video), .jpg/.png (image), .exe (executable), .zip (compressed).

Options: B) Prepares it for use by creating a file system (erases all data)
Explanation: Formatting: prepares storage by creating file system (NTFS, FAT32, exFAT) and erasing all data. High-level format: creates file system. Low-level format: manufacturer's process marking sectors.

Options: B) File system used in Windows
Explanation: NTFS (New Technology File System): Windows default file system. Supports large files, permissions, encryption, journaling. FAT32: older, cross-platform, limited to 4GB per file. exFAT: for flash drives.

Options: A) Shuts down the computer immediately
Explanation: Ctrl+Alt+Delete: opens security screen with options: Lock, Switch User, Sign out, Change password, Task Manager. Ctrl+Shift+Escape: opens Task Manager directly.

Options: B) Running processes, CPU/memory usage, and allows terminating programs
Explanation: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc): shows running processes, performance (CPU, RAM, disk, network usage), startup programs, services. Can end unresponsive programs ('End Task').

Options: B) Software that allows OS to communicate with hardware devices
Explanation: Device driver: software translating OS commands to hardware-specific instructions. Printer driver, graphics driver, sound driver. Without correct driver, hardware won't function properly.

Options: B) Open-source OS (free, modifiable source code)
Explanation: Linux: open-source OS (kernel created by Linus Torvalds, 1991). Free, customisable. Distributions: Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, CentOS, Kali. Used in servers, Android (Linux kernel), supercomputers.

Options: A) One job at a time interactively
B) Jobs collected in batches and processed without user interaction
Explanation: Batch processing: collects jobs into a batch, processes automatically without user interaction. Early mainframe computing. Still used for: payroll, bank statement generation, bill processing.

Options: B) Moving processes between RAM and disk (virtual memory mechanism)
Explanation: Swapping: when RAM is full, OS moves inactive process/data to swap space (disk) → frees RAM for active processes → swaps back when needed. Slower than RAM but extends available memory.

Options: A) A list of Windows users
B) Hierarchical database storing OS and application configuration settings
C) A backup of system files
D) A list of installed hardware
Explanation: Windows Registry: central database storing configuration for OS and applications. HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, etc. Edited with Registry Editor (regedit) — dangerous if misused.

QuestionText: 'Safe Mode' in Windows starts the OS with:
Options: B) Minimal drivers and programs (for troubleshooting)
Explanation: Safe Mode: starts Windows with minimal drivers and services. Used to diagnose/fix problems. No unnecessary drivers, no startup programs, basic VGA display. Access by pressing F8 at startup.

Options: B) Reorganises fragmented data for faster access
Explanation: Defragmentation: rearranges fragmented file pieces into contiguous storage → improves HDD read speed. Not needed for SSDs (they have no moving parts). Windows: Optimise Drives.
BIOS: firmware stored in ROM on motherboard. Performs POST (Power-On Self-Test), initialises hardware, loads the OS bootloader. Modern replacement: UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface).

QuestionText: Which of these is an interactive (time-sharing) OS?
Options: B) Windows, Linux — respond immediately to user input
Explanation: Interactive/time-sharing OS: gives each user/process a time slice of CPU. Responds to input immediately. Windows, Linux, macOS are interactive OS. Users perceive instantaneous response.

Options: A) Copies of the original file
B) Pointers/links to the original file or program
Explanation: Shortcut: a small file pointing to the original. Deleting shortcut doesn't delete original. Identified by arrow on icon. Used to access programs/files quickly from Desktop/taskbar.

Options: B) Asks for permission before allowing programs to make system changes
Explanation: UAC: security feature prompting for confirmation/admin password before allowing programs to make significant system changes. Prevents malware from making unauthorised changes silently.

QuestionText: 'Kernel' is the __ of an operating system.
Options: B) Core/heart that manages hardware resources directly
Explanation: Kernel: core of OS. Manages: CPU scheduling, memory management, device I/O, system calls. Directly interacts with hardware. Everything else (shell, applications) sits on top of kernel.

QuestionText: The Windows 'Start Menu' provides access to:
Options: B) Installed applications, settings, search, and power options
Explanation: Start Menu (Windows button): access point for apps, search, settings, documents, power (sleep, restart, shutdown). Pinned and recently used apps displayed. Open with Windows key.

Options: B) Recently cut or copied data (text, images, files) for pasting
Explanation: Clipboard: temporary memory holding cut/copied content. Ctrl+C = Copy, Ctrl+X = Cut (to clipboard), Ctrl+V = Paste. Windows 10+ clipboard history: Win+V shows clipboard history.

Options: A) Multiple programs on one computer
B) Multiple users to access system simultaneously
C) One user at a time only
D) Multiple computers to share one monitor
Explanation: Multi-user OS: Linux, Unix, mainframe OS. Multiple users simultaneously access the system, each with own files/settings. Network/mainframe environments. Windows also supports multiple user accounts.

Options: B) CPU accesses a page not currently in RAM (must be loaded from disk)
Explanation: Page fault: accessed memory page not in RAM → OS must load it from disk (swap space) → slower. Many page faults = 'thrashing' → system becomes very slow. Solution: more RAM.

QuestionText: The process of starting or restarting a computer is called:
Explanation: Booting: starting up computer. Cold boot: from powered off state. Warm boot: restart without full power off (Ctrl+Alt+Delete or Start→Restart). BIOS/UEFI → bootloader → OS loads.

Options: A) Physically cleans the hard drive
B) Removes temporary files, system files to free up disk space
Explanation: Disk Cleanup: removes temp files, cached files, Recycle Bin contents, old Windows Update files. Frees up disk space. Access via right-click drive → Properties → Disk Cleanup.

QuestionText: In Windows file system, 'root directory' is:
Options: B) The top-most directory (C:\) from which all other directories branch
Explanation: Root directory: top level of file system hierarchy. Windows: C:\ (or D:\). Unix/Linux: / All other directories are subdirectories of root. Tree structure branches from root.

QuestionText: Which Windows 7 feature allows you to pin programmes to the taskbar?
Explanation: Pin to Taskbar: right-click a programme shortcut or running programme's taskbar icon → 'Pin to taskbar'. Keeps it there for quick access. Unpin: right-click → 'Unpin from taskbar'.

Options: B) Allows snapping windows to screen edges/corners for side-by-side view
Explanation: Snap (Aero Snap): drag window to screen edge → snaps to half/quarter screen. Or Win+Left/Right arrow. Allows easy side-by-side multitasking. Windows 7 introduced basic snap; Windows 10/11 improved it.

QuestionText: A 'directory' in OS terminology is same as:
Options: B) A folder (container for files and other folders)
Explanation: Directory = folder. A container that organises files and subdirectories. 'Directory' is Unix/Linux term; 'Folder' is Windows GUI term. Same concept.

Options: B) Transparent glass effect, Aero Peek, Shake, Snap
Explanation: Aero (Windows Vista/7): glass-like transparent window borders, Aero Peek (show desktop preview), Aero Shake (shake window to minimise others), Aero Snap (window docking). Requires capable GPU.

Options: A) Turns off the monitor only
B) Saves RAM contents to disk and powers off completely (resumes quickly)
C) Puts computer in low-power mode keeping RAM active
Explanation: Hibernate: saves RAM state to disk file (hiberfil.sys) → powers off. Resumes quickly to exact previous state. vs Sleep: keeps RAM powered (faster resume but uses electricity).

Options: B) System/configuration files not shown by default (to prevent accidental changes)
Explanation: Hidden files: not displayed by default in File Explorer. Usually system files. View hidden files: Folder Options → View → 'Show hidden files'. Common hidden files: .ini, pagefile.sys.

QuestionText: The 'PATH' environment variable in OS stores:
Options: B) List of directories searched when running commands in terminal
C) Network path of shared drives
Explanation: PATH: environment variable listing directories where OS looks for executable programs when you type a command. Without correct PATH, commands not found. E.g., Python, Java added to PATH for terminal use.

Options: B) Reverts system to a previous restore point without affecting personal files
C) Backs up files to cloud
Explanation: System Restore: reverts OS settings/registry to a previous restore point (created before changes/installs). Doesn't delete personal files but removes recently installed programs. Good for fixing software issues.

Options: B) Storing print jobs in queue before sending to printer
Explanation: Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online): stores print jobs in a queue (spool). Computer sends jobs to spool quickly; printer processes at its slower speed. Allows computer to continue working.

QuestionText: Which Windows shortcut takes a screenshot?
Options: B) Alt+Print Screen (active window) or Print Screen (full screen)
Explanation: Print Screen (PrtScn): captures full screen to clipboard. Alt+Print Screen: captures only active window. Win+Shift+S: Snip & Sketch tool. Win+Print Screen: saves screenshot as file.

Options: B) Logs system events, errors, warnings for diagnostics
D) Tracks user activity for billing
Explanation: Event Viewer: shows detailed logs of system events (Application, Security, System). Useful for diagnosing crashes, driver errors, login events, failed operations. Accessed via Control Panel or search.

Options: B) A program fails to release memory it no longer needs, gradually consuming all RAM
C) Disk space being used up
Explanation: Memory leak: program allocates memory but doesn't free it when done. Memory usage grows over time → system slows → eventually crashes. Common in programs with poor memory management. Fixed by closing/restarting program.

Options: A) Provides access to local library databases
B) Virtual folders that aggregate content from multiple locations into one view
Explanation: Libraries (Windows 7+): virtual folders that collect content from multiple locations (local + network). Documents Library includes My Documents + Public Documents. Simplifies file management.

Options: A) Devices require manual driver installation
B) Devices automatically detected and configured by OS when connected
Explanation: Plug and Play (PnP): connect device → OS automatically detects, installs drivers, configures. USB devices are PnP. Introduced with Windows 95 — previously all hardware needed manual configuration.

QuestionText: Which type of OS serves requests from multiple computers on a network?
Explanation: Network/Server OS: designed to manage and share resources on a network. Examples: Windows Server, Linux server distributions. Handles user accounts, file sharing, web hosting, database services.
